newsitem.title: USA: CME hogs, bellies end limit up again on Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: CME hogs, bellies end limit up again on Taiwan.

text.p: April through August CME hog futures and May pork belly futures posted limit gains at the close for the second consecutive day on bullish ideas U.S. pork exports will increase to fill a void left by Taiwan's exit from the world market.
New contract highs were also set in deferred hog contracts, traders noted.

Hogs closed up the 2.000-cent-per-lb limit to 0.250 higher with April limit up at 72.275 cents. October and February through July 1998 contracts posted new contract highs with October 1997 climbing to 69.350 cents before settling 1.875 cent higher at 69.325 cents. Pork bellies ended 3.000 to 1.400 higher with May limit up at 79.300 cents.
Anticipation U.S. pork exports will rise on the Taiwan problem kept short covering demand strong, traders said.
"A lot of what we are seeing here is just blatant short covering," said Dale Durchholz, marketing analyst for AgriVisor Services Inc.
Pork exports have not increased yet, but the speculation is that much of Taiwan's pork sales to Japan and South Korea will be partly made up by U.S. pork.
Pork values have already started to rise as packers build stocks and hog producers are also raising asking prices, traders and analysts said.
Chris Goldthwait, USDA's general sales manager, also said Friday there could be an increase in U.S. pork exports to traditional Taiwan customers.

Taiwan banned exports of pork due to the outbreak and Japan, its biggest customer, and South Korea imposed indefinite bans on imports of Taiwan pork. Japan had been importing about 16,000 tonnes of Taiwan fresh and frozen pork per month.

Taiwan need for feed grains will also be down which is easing feed costs and should encourage U.S. hog producers to hold back more hogs for breeding. This could add to already firming cash hog markets as producers hold back breeding stock to increase hog numbers. Cash hogs are called at least $1 to $2 higher on Monday, traders said.

But Durchholz noted that April futures already hold a large premium to cash and domestic retail demand still accounts for the overwhelming percentage of pork consumption from U.S. packing plants. The USDA Hog and Pigs report next Thursday may also be of great importance to pork markets if it shows already increasing hog numbers.

Early analyst estimates on the report indicated all hogs on U.S. farms at 97 to 100.6 percent of a year ago and hogs kept for breeding estimates were running from 98.5 to as much as 104 percent of a year ago. Early hogs kept for market estimates ranged from 97 to 110.8 percent.
March pork bellies eased late and only May remained at limit up as the market awaited the monthly USDA Cold Storage report to be released after the close, traders said.
Estimates on USDA's storage report ranged from 41.2 to 43.0 million lbs on hand March 1.

After the close, USDA reported there were 43.881 million lbs of bellies in storage February 28, slightly more than the estimate and above 38.04 million on hand last month. The figure was above 46.38 million on hand March 1, 1996.

Analysts called the USDA report neutral for hog and pork belly futures on Monday, saying the Taiwan news and expectations ahead of the Hogs and Pigs report Thursday will overshadow the Cold Storage Report.
There were 600 unfilled buy orders in April hogs at the close with showing 300 buy orders. May bellies at 100 left to buy at limit up, pit sources said.

In options trade, the April hog synthetic close at 73.000 and June at 80.650 while the May belly synthetic was at 79.500. Pit sourcs noted solid call bids in hog options all day with volatility of five percent in April and off two percent in other months.
